This paper presents a photonic hardware accelerator for solving combinatorial optimization problems (Ising model, Max-Cut) using annealing algorithms. The core contribution is computational: implementing optimization algorithms with novel photonic hardware to achieve algorithmic speedup. The programmable photonic processor is the implementation substrate, not the research target. The work focuses on algorithm performance (success probability >80%, scalability to N=50), error analysis affecting computational outcomes, and benchmark optimization problems. Per rule 8, computer architecture alone doesn't qualify unless novelty is pure algorithms—here the novelty is the algorithmic acceleration approach using reconfigurable matrix multiplication for iterative Hamiltonian computation. The photonic implementation serves the algorithmic optimization goal. This maps to 'Algorithms & Computational Complexity: Algorithm design, complexity analysis, graph algorithms, parallel algorithms, and optimization methods for computational problems' rather than quantum photonics (which focuses on quantum light generation, entanglement, quantum states) or general photonic devices (which focus on optical component engineering). The Ising machine is fundamentally an optimization algorithm accelerator.

NOT Development Economics which focuses on poverty, inequality, welfare schemes, and livelihood outcomes.

The work involves interferometric measurement methods and spatial coherence characterization, which falls squarely within optical metrology instrumentation rather than Direction of Arrival & Beamforming (which is focused on antenna arrays and signal processing for wireless/RF systems). The interferometric technique for source separation is a metrology application, not a beamforming/DOA estimation problem in the communication systems sense.

Biomedical target application is secondary to the materials-level energy conversion mechanisms. RIS-assisted ambient backscatter communication (AmBC) with energy harvesting is fundamentally a cooperative/relay communication architecture. The RIS acts as a passive relay/cooperative element that assists the communication link by intelligently reflecting RF signals to enable low-power backscatter transmission. The paper addresses relay-like cooperative multiplexing through RIS element allocation, performance analysis of relay-assisted systems (outage probability, achievable rate), and resource optimization in cooperative networks. While signal modulation and detection are involved, the core contribution centers on the cooperative relay architecture (RIS-assisted AmBC) rather than novel modulation/detection/equalization techniques. The finite blocklength aspect is an analysis framework, not the primary architectural novelty. Best fit: Cooperative & Relay Networks.
